opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really interesting experiment, and honestly I see it more as a signal than a finished product.

What it's trying to do is put an agent at the operating-system level, so the model isn't just a chatbot inside one app. It can actually look at the screen, understand what's going on, and operate across apps for you. Conceptually, that's the direction a lot of us believe in. If models are going to be useful in daily life, they eventually need to act, not just answer. The phone is the device people use most, so it's a very natural place to try.

From a research perspective, the hard part isn't the demo. Getting an agent to book something or compare prices once in a controlled setting is doable now. The hard part is reliability across the long tail: weird UI layouts, pop-ups, login states, apps that change every week. Users have very little tolerance for an agent that works 80% of the time when it's touching their money or their messages. So I'd judge it less on how impressive the first impression is and more on how the success rate on real, messy tasks improves over time.

There's also an ecosystem question that isn't really technical. Many apps don't want an outside agent operating them, because it bypasses their interface, their ads, and their control over the user relationship. So you quickly run into friction with platforms, and that may decide how far this goes more than the model quality does.

So my overall view is that the direction is right and it's brave to ship something this early, but it's still the early, slightly awkward stage. The real test is whether it becomes something people rely on every day, rather than something they try a few times because it's cool.

r002.rationale: It does not say that an agent’s execution cost exceeding the task’s value is unacceptable.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll be honest that I'm looking at it more as a researcher than as someone who's spent weeks using it as a daily driver, so take this with that caveat.

I think the most interesting thing about the Doubao phone isn't the model. The model is roughly what you'd expect. What's interesting is that it's a bet on where the agent lives. For the last couple of years, most agent products have lived inside a chat box. You open an app, you type, something happens inside that app. The phone is saying: the agent should sit at the system level, it should be able to see the screen and touch the screen, and it should operate the apps you already have rather than asking every app to build its own AI feature.

From a research point of view, I like that framing, because it matches what I've been saying about the second half. The bottleneck now is much less about whether the model can reason and much more about the environment and the interface. A phone is actually a very good environment. It's constrained, the action space is small, taps and swipes and typing, and the tasks are extremely well-defined and high frequency. Order me a coffee, book this, reply to that message. That's a much better place to make an agent useful than, say, a wide-open browser.

Where I'm more skeptical is on two things. The first is reliability. A demo that works nine times out of ten is a great demo and a bad product. If it mis-taps on a payment screen once, you stop trusting it, and trust is the whole product here. I don't think anyone, including ByteDance, has fully solved the long-tail of UI states yet, and I'd want to see real failure rates rather than curated clips.

The second is the incentive problem, which is not a technical problem. If the agent operates apps on your behalf, the apps themselves lose control of the interaction, and the app companies have every reason to push back, block it, or make their interfaces hostile to automation. We've already seen some of that. So the phone becomes a kind of platform fight, and whether it wins depends more on distribution and ecosystem politics than on the model.

So my overall assessment: as a product, it's an early and somewhat rough version of something that I think is clearly the right direction. As a signal, it's quite important, because it tells you the big players have moved from "chat" to "act," and they're willing to go down to the OS layer to do it. I'd rather see this kind of attempt than another chat app, even if the first version is not great.

astra-6.text:
我会先看它到底解决了什么问题。如果只是把聊天入口放到手机里，让你更方便地问问题，那它的价值还是一个助手。更值得期待的是，它能不能把用户的一句话，变成跨应用执行的一件事。

比如你说“帮我安排一下明天的出行”，这里面可能涉及日历、地图、订票，还有最后的确认。难点不只是模型理解你说了什么，而是它有没有足够的上下文和操作权限，执行过程中出错了能不能恢复，以及什么时候应该停下来问你。

所以我觉得这个方向很值得探索，但具体到豆包手机这个产品，仅凭我们现在聊到的信息，我还不能判断它做得怎么样。我会特别关注：用户试过几次之后，会不会持续把真实任务交给它。如果每一步都要盯着，最后自己操作反而更快，那能力展示和产品价值之间就还有距离。真正有价值的时候，是用户能够放心地把一部分事情交出去。

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate two questions: is it a good phone, and is it a good way to explore an AI-native device? Those aren’t necessarily the same thing.

For me, the interesting question is whether the assistant can actually complete tasks across applications. If I still have to open each app, find the right page, and tell it exactly what to do, then we’ve mostly added another interface. The bigger change would be letting me express an intention and having the system handle the intermediate steps.

But that also raises the bar for reliability. A conversation can tolerate an imperfect answer; an assistant taking actions needs to understand permissions, recognize uncertainty, and let you recover when something goes wrong.

So I wouldn’t judge it primarily by how impressive a demonstration looks. I’d ask: after a few weeks, which tasks do people consistently delegate to it? How often do they have to intervene? Does it actually save effort? That’s what would make it a meaningful product.
